135.subtitle: Treasury, army, empire, and the ocean at the border

commentary.meaning: This verse finishes what the last one began, and it finishes it by inventory. Classical Indian political theory analyses a state into constituent elements — the ruler, the counsel, the territory, the stronghold, the treasury, the armed force — and the first four names here work down that list: the fortune that attaches to rule, the treasury, the fourfold army, and finally paramount empire itself. The alliteration on rāj that dominated the previous verse runs out after the first name and is replaced by a run on s, so the ear registers a handover even before the sense changes. And it does change. Satyasandhā, whose pledge holds good, is not another asset but the guarantee behind all of them; a giver of empires is worth nothing unless her word is good, and the verse says so at exactly the point where the promises have become extravagant. The last name then stops describing what she owns and describes what she is. Girdled by the ocean is what poets say of the earth, and applying it to her converts the whole preceding inventory: the territory is not her possession but her body.
commentary.history:
Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra analyses the state into seven constituent limbs — the sovereign, the minister, the countryside, the fortified capital, the treasury, the coercive force, and the ally — and the scheme was common property across the Sanskrit literature on statecraft. Two of the seven, kośa and bala, are named here in succession, with rājya and sāmrājya framing them. Whether or not the composer had a particular manual in mind, the vocabulary is technical rather than merely grand: it is what a court poet would use to praise an actual king. The hymn is not straining for metaphor. It is applying the ordinary language of sovereignty to the goddess and letting the application do the work.

Rājyalakṣmī, the fortune of kingship, names something Indian tradition treats as an independent power rather than a quality of the ruler. Śrī or Lakṣmī confers sovereignty by choosing to reside with a king, and — this is what gives the idea its edge — she may leave. The narrative literature is full of her migrations: she is churned out of the ocean of milk, she attends the demon Bali during his ascendancy and departs when he is dispossessed, and a kingdom's decline is described as her withdrawal. To call her rājyalakṣmī is therefore to name the volatile element in political power, the thing no amount of administration can secure. That she is churned from the sea also makes a quiet frame for the verse, which ends on the ocean.

Kośa is a word of unusual range. Its base sense is a container — a chest, a cask, a scabbard, the calyx of a flower — and from there the state treasury, and also a lexicon, which is why the standard Sanskrit thesaurus is the Amarakośa, a treasure-chest of words. Vedānta gives it a further use. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad's second section describes the self as wrapped in a series of sheaths, from the one made of food outward through breath, mind and understanding to the one made of bliss, and the later tradition calls these the five kośas. A reader who takes kośanāthā only as mistress of the treasury has the plain sense right; one who hears the Vedāntic term as well has her presiding over the five envelopes in which a human being is packed. Both are traditional, and this hymn is normally happy to intend both.

Caturaṅgabala is the standard designation of a complete army: four aṅgas or limbs, being elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry. The phrase has an afterlife most readers will recognise without knowing it: the board game caturaṅga, named for those four arms, travelled west through Persian shatranj and became chess. Her forces in the surrounding narrative are described in exactly these terms; caturaṅgabaleśvarī certifies that the army is complete and that she, not Daṇḍanāthā, commands it.

Sāmrājya is a stronger word than rājya, and the strength is old. Vedic ritual literature distinguishes grades of rulership, associating different consecration rites with different titles, and the accounts of the great anointing preserve a graded list of paramount conditions — sāmrājya, bhaujya, svārājya and others — with imperial paramountcy at its head. Commentators on this hymn take a standing interest in svārājya, self-rule, reading the gift of empire as sovereignty over oneself. The reading is legitimate, but the hymn itself says sāmrājya, and the tradition has never much wanted to choose.

Satyasandhā is the hinge. Sandhā, from sam plus √dhā, to put together, is a compact, something laid down between parties; satyasandha, one whose engagements hold, is a standing epithet of Rāma in the Rāmāyaṇa. Applied here, after four names promising treasure, force and empire, it converts the promises into obligations. The Śākta tradition has a specific pledge in view: at the close of the Devī Māhātmya the goddess undertakes to become manifest again whenever the world is oppressed by demonic power, and the cult of her repeated advent rests on it. Satyasandhā says that it is not rhetoric.

Sāgaramekhalā, she whose girdle is the ocean, is a poetic commonplace redirected. The earth is regularly called ocean-girdled, and a cakravartin's domain conventionally has no border but water. Attached to her, the epithet does two things at once. It completes the political series, since ocean-to-ocean is the largest kingdom there is, and it dissolves it, since a person wearing the sea as a belt is not a ruler of the earth but the earth itself. The verse has been listing what she commands, and it ends by relocating all of it inside her.
commentary.practice:
The verse divides evenly and unusually: four syllables, four, eight in the first line; six, four, six in the second. The two eight-syllable names sit at the ends of their lines, which gives the whole verse a rocking motion, short units gathering into a long one. Where the previous verse hammered on rāj, this one begins with rājyalakṣmīḥ and then abandons the pattern for a run of s: sāmrājyadāyinī, satyasandhā, sāgaramekhalā.

Rājyalakṣmīḥ contains the conjunct kṣm, which frightens people unnecessarily. Kṣ is a single unit in practice, made at the back of the mouth and released as a sibilant, and the m follows it directly; lakṣmī is two syllables, lak-ṣmī, not three. The name also ends in a visarga, and this is a small grammatical curiosity worth knowing: most feminine stems in long ī, like devī and nadī, have no ending in the nominative singular, but lakṣmī takes one, which is why the hymn reads lakṣmīḥ rather than lakṣmī.

Caturaṅgabaleśvarī has the nasal ṅ before g, which is the sound English has at the end of sing, and it must be that nasal and not the dental n. The name also hides a sandhi: bala ends in short a, īśvarī begins in long ī, and a plus ī yields e, so baleśvarī is bala plus īśvarī. Seeing that keeps the word from having to be memorised as an undifferentiated string, and the same join reappears throughout the hymn.

In satyasandhā the cluster ndh is a dental n followed by an aspirated dental dh, and the aspiration must be heard. In sāgaramekhalā there is nothing difficult, which makes it the natural place to let the line settle; it is the last name of the verse and the metre gives it room.

Chanted as archanā with each name in the dative followed by namaḥ, the verse once again mixes stem classes and once again punishes the assumption that everything ends in -āyai. The ā-stems give kośanāthāyai, satyasandhāyai, sāgaramekhalāyai. The ī-stems contract: rājyalakṣmyai, caturaṅgabaleśvaryai, sāmrājyadāyinyai. Three and three, alternating irregularly, so this verse is worth rehearsing slowly in the nāmāvalī form before it is taken at speed.

The difficulty this verse presents is not phonetic but dispositional. It is a list of very large worldly goods, and it is being chanted, in most cases, by someone who will not receive an empire. Two responses to that have long coexisted in the tradition, and neither requires embarrassment. The first is to take the names as they stand and understand that the hymn was composed in and for a world where kingdoms were real objects of petition and the goddess was a state deity. The other is to follow the commentators to svārājya and hear the treasury as the sheaths of the self and the empire as self-possession. What the verse itself supplies, in the fifth name, is the reason either reading can be trusted: what she has undertaken she performs. And what the sixth supplies is the correction against grasping, since once the earth turns out to be her body there is nothing left that could be received from outside.

crossReferences.iast: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata | abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmy aham ||
crossReferences.translation: Whenever there is a flagging of dharma, Bhārata, and a rising up of what is contrary to it, then I bring myself forth.
crossReferences.relevance: The most famous divine undertaking in Sanskrit literature, and the best gloss on satyasandhā. What makes a pledge of this kind meaningful is not its grandeur but the assurance that it will be honoured without further petition, which is precisely what the compound asserts: her sandhā is satya, so the promise is already as good as performed. The Śākta tradition has its own version of this pledge at the close of the Devī Māhātmya, where the goddess undertakes to manifest again whenever the world is oppressed, and the sahasranāma's name is best read against both.

crossReferences.translation: In the middle of an ocean of nectar, on a jewel island ringed with groves of the trees of heaven, in a house of wish-granting stone set in a garden of kadamba, on a couch whose frame is Śiva, resting on the bed that is the supreme Śiva — a fortunate few worship you there, wave of consciousness and bliss.
crossReferences.relevance: The other side of sāgaramekhalā. Here the ocean is not a border she wears but the water around the island where she is enthroned, and the verse gives the royal imagery of this whole passage its setting: an island capital, a jewelled house, a couch. Read together, the two images describe the same geography from outside and inside — the sea at the edge of an emperor's territory, and the sea surrounding the palace at its centre.

references.title: King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra
references.author: tr. Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 2013)
references.note: The current standard translation, with an introduction that untangles the text's layers. Read the opening books on the constituent elements of the state, and kośa and bala will stop looking like poetic ornament in this verse and start looking like the two things a functioning government was understood to consist of.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: tr. Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: For the second reading of kośanāthā. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad's account of the self wrapped in successive envelopes — food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss — is short, strange and much less systematic than the later fivefold scheme built on it, and reading it in the original order is the only way to see how much the tradition added.

references.title: Invoking Lakshmi: The Goddess of Wealth in Song and Ceremony
references.author: Constantina Rhodes (SUNY Press, 2010)
references.note: Useful for rājyalakṣmī specifically. Rhodes translates a body of Lakṣmī liturgy and is clear-eyed about the fact that these are prayers for money and status, which is the right frame for a verse that promises treasuries and empires without apologising for it.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library and Research Centre)
references.note: The place to see the commentarial move from sāmrājya to svārājya performed rather than described. Whether or not you accept the readings, the method — plain sense first, then a second sense drawn from Vedāntic or ritual vocabulary — is the tradition's own, and this verse gives it plenty to work with.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Sir Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up kośa and read the entry to the end. Chest, scabbard, flower-bud, treasury, dictionary, and the sheath of the self all sit under one headword, and the spread explains why a single name in this verse can be heard by two readers in two entirely different registers without either being wrong.
